scenes.visual: Title card 'Change Lives on the Branches' over the same five-tip tree from the first film. THE WORLD, kept for both films (16:9, warm cream background). One horizontal tree, root on the left, tips on the right, five tips top to bottom: lamprey, shark, trout, frog, human, each with a simple flat cartoon icon (no photographs). Internal nodes are small circles labelled R (root), J, B, T. COLOUR MAP, same in every scene of both films: branches dark charcoal; node B GOLD (the trout-human most recent common ancestor); node J GREY-BLUE; nodes R and T plain charcoal; a derived state TEAL; an ancestral state light GREY; trace lines from tips back to nodes are the colour of the node they reach. A thin time arrow under the tree points right, labelled 'older' at the left and 'today' at the right. Tree drawings are schematic, not to time scale. In this film each tip carries a small state badge: GREY = ancestral state, TEAL = derived state. Change marks are short TEAL ticks across a branch (a gain) or GREY ticks (a loss). A tally counter sits at the top right.

scenes.tts: The first film read relatedness at the nodes. This one follows the animals' features. Sharks and humans both have jaws. Did they get them from one ancestor, or twice?
scenes.visual: The first film's tree, with GOLD node B and GREY-BLUE node J. Jaw icons appear on the shark and human tips, with a question mark between them.
scenes.narration: The first film read relatedness at the nodes. This one follows the animals' features. Sharks and humans both have jaws. Did they get them from one ancestor, or twice?

scenes.tts: A character is a feature that varies among taxa, like jaws. Its forms are its states: jaws present, or jaws absent. A change of state happens somewhere along a branch.
scenes.visual: A label 'character: jaws' slides in. Two badges: TEAL 'jaws present', GREY 'jaws absent'. A small TEAL tick slides along one branch to show 'change happens on a branch'.
scenes.narration: A character is a feature that varies among taxa, like jaws. Its forms are its states: jaws present, or jaws absent. A change of state happens somewhere along a branch.

scenes.tts: Which state came first? Take the outgroup's state as the starting point. Lamprey has no jaws, so absence is the ancestral state. That is an assumption, since the outgroup's lineage can change too.
scenes.visual: The lamprey tip gets a GREY 'no jaws' badge; a GREY wash flows from lamprey back to the root R, labelled 'starting state (from the outgroup)'. A small footnote tag: 'assumption'.
scenes.narration: Which state came first? Take the outgroup's state as the starting point. Lamprey has no jaws, so absence is the ancestral state. That is an assumption, since the outgroup's lineage can change too.

scenes.tts: Shark, trout, frog and human all have jaws. One gain, on the branch from the root to node J, explains all five tips. So, on this mapping, jaws in sharks and humans are homologous. That means similar because of a single origin in a common ancestor.
scenes.visual: TEAL badges appear on shark, trout, frog and human. A single TEAL tick lands on the branch from R to J; TEAL flows down every branch to the right of J. Tally shows '1 change'. Label 'homology: one origin'.
scenes.narration: Shark, trout, frog and human all have jaws. One gain, on the branch from the root to node J, explains all five tips. So, on this mapping, jaws in sharks and humans are homologous. That means similar because of a single origin in a common ancestor.

scenes.tts: Parsimony prefers the mapping that needs the fewest changes. It is a rule for choosing among explanations. It does not claim that evolution takes the shortest path.
scenes.visual: A balance-scale icon labelled 'parsimony' tips toward the card '1 change' and away from a faded card showing several ticks. Small text: 'a rule for choosing, not a law of evolution'.
scenes.narration: Parsimony prefers the mapping that needs the fewest changes. It is a rule for choosing among explanations. It does not claim that evolution takes the shortest path.

scenes.tts: Now a made-up character, called X. Trout and human have it. Lamprey, shark and frog do not. Again, absence is the starting state.
scenes.visual: Jaw badges clear. New badges labelled 'X (made up)': TEAL on trout and human; GREY on lamprey, shark and frog. Tally resets to 0.
scenes.narration: Now a made-up character, called X. Trout and human have it. Lamprey, shark and frog do not. Again, absence is the starting state.

scenes.tts: Here is one mapping. X is gained on the branch into node B, then lost on the branch to frog. That is one origin, so trout and human share X by homology.
scenes.visual: Panel A, labelled 'one origin'. A TEAL tick lands on the branch from J into the GOLD node B; TEAL flows to trout, frog and human; then a GREY tick lands on frog's branch and frog's badge turns GREY. Tally counter beside panel A ticks once per mark, left hidden under a card.
scenes.narration: Here is one mapping. X is gained on the branch into node B, then lost on the branch to frog. That is one origin, so trout and human share X by homology.

scenes.tts: Here is another. X is gained twice, once on the branch to trout and once on the branch to human. That is convergence. It means similarity that arose independently in separate lineages.
scenes.visual: Panel B, labelled 'two origins', appears beside panel A, same tree. One TEAL tick on trout's own branch, one on human's own branch. Its tally also ticks under a hidden card.
scenes.narration: Here is another. X is gained twice, once on the branch to trout and once on the branch to human. That is convergence. It means similarity that arose independently in separate lineages.

scenes.tts: Which mapping does parsimony prefer? Count the marks on each tree in your head. What is the fewest changes that could explain X?
scenes.visual: Panels A and B side by side, both tallies covered. Question card: 'Fewest changes for X?'
scenes.narration: Which mapping does parsimony prefer? Count the marks on each tree in your head. What is the fewest changes that could explain X?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; a 7-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Each needs two changes. No single branch leads to trout and human alone, so one change cannot do it. A gain on the branch into node J, with two losses, would need three.
scenes.visual: Both tally cards flip: panel A '2', panel B '2'. A third small panel C flashes: TEAL tick on R to J, GREY ticks on shark and frog, tally '3', then fades. On screen: 'minimum = 2'.
scenes.narration: Each needs two changes. No single branch leads to trout and human alone, so one change cannot do it. A gain on the branch into node J, with two losses, would need three.

scenes.tts: So the two mappings tie. Parsimony alone cannot choose between one origin and two. Homology or convergence stays an open question.
scenes.visual: Panels A and B slide together under a banner 'tie'. The balance-scale icon sits level between them.
scenes.narration: So the two mappings tie. Parsimony alone cannot choose between one origin and two. Homology or convergence stays an open question.

scenes.tts: To break the tie, you need more evidence. How X develops, or what genes build it. Fossils with intermediate states. Or more taxa on the tree.
scenes.visual: Three icon cards fan out under the tie: 'development and genes' (a schematic embryo outline), 'fossils with intermediate states' (a schematic fossil slab), 'more taxa' (an empty dashed tip slot added to the tree, with no badge).
scenes.narration: To break the tie, you need more evidence. How X develops, or what genes build it. Fossils with intermediate states. Or more taxa on the tree.

scenes.tts: So map every change onto a branch. Two taxa share a state by homology when both inherit it from one gain on a shared branch. Other lineages may later lose it. Separate gains are convergence.
scenes.visual: Back to the jaws tree: the single TEAL tick on the branch from R to J pulses, with shark and human badges glowing TEAL. Then panel A of X flashes back, its frog loss tick in GREY. Text: 'one gain on a shared branch = one origin; later losses allowed'.
scenes.narration: So map every change onto a branch. Two taxa share a state by homology when both inherit it from one gain on a shared branch. Other lineages may later lose it. Separate gains are convergence.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex holding a small tick-marked branch. Line: 'One gain on a shared branch means one origin.'
